name: Vera Gupta

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for meeting me, Vera. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and what you say here is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you actually think. To start, what does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a fit-out carpenter for a subcontractor, so I do the insides of buildings once the shell's up: metal stud partitions, plasterboard, suspended ceilings, door sets. This month it's a secondary school extension, twelve classrooms, about fifty minutes' drive from home. I leave at six, so Tom does the school run with our two. Lots of measuring, lots of screwing board, and a lot of waiting for the electricians to finish so we can close up.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What keeps you in it, and what wears you down?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that it's tidy work. You walk into a concrete box on Monday and by Friday it's a corridor with doors and a ceiling, and the teachers will never know who did it. What wears me down is that it's both of us in construction. Tom's a self-employed electrician, so when building slows down, we both feel it at once, and we've got less than a month put by.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say well, that's that then, and get back to work. I'd probably make a joke in the site group chat about the robots not turning up. Nothing much to say beyond that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it's fine. I use the AI on my phone now and then, mostly to turn a drawing measurement into board sizes or to help Kai with his science homework. If that's all it does, good.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on. I'd keep doing the fit-out, keep the bills paid, and try again to put a little aside each month. Tom might use it a bit more for his quotes, that'd save him evenings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A tiny bit relieved, maybe, because one less thing to think about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said 'try again' to put a little aside. What usually gets in the way?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Something always comes up. Last year it was the car's clutch, the year before Tom had a month with no jobs. We start a pot and then the pot gets eaten.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would anything bother you, even in this calm version?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That both our jobs depend on the same thing, people building. AI or no AI, if interest rates go up and the builders stop, we're both out. That's the risk I think about, not robots.

S0.say: She'd shrug, say 'that's that then' and get back to work, maybe with a joke in the site group chat about robots not turning up.
S0.think: It's fine for her: she uses AI now and then to convert drawing measurements and help her son with homework. If that's all it does, that's good.
S0.do: Carries on with fit-out work, keeps the bills paid and tries once again to save a little each month. Expects her partner might use AI more for his quotes.
S0.feel: Calm and a little relieved to have one less thing to think about.
S0.quote: We start a pot and then the pot gets eaten.
S0.fieldNote: Vera is practical and unflappable here. Her real structural worry is that both household incomes depend on construction, which she raises herself. AI is just one more tool to her, used now and then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's going to change how we work, so we'd better keep up. I don't think it's good or bad, it just is. Firms should help people train and the government should help those who get caught out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I've already seen a video of a machine that puts up plasterboard on its own. If they get good, the boarding is half my day. I'm not going to panic, but I'm not going to pretend it won't touch me either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait until I saw one on a real site, then I'd ask to be the person who works alongside it, setting out, checking, finishing the edges it can't do. I'd ask the subcontractor whether they'd pay for training. And I'd talk to Tom about him learning the controls side of new buildings, smart systems, because that's going to need electricians.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Like a draught under the door you know you'll have to fix eventually.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait to see one on a real site. What would convince you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Seeing it do a whole floor without someone babysitting it. Plenty of things look great in a video. Then on site you find out it can't handle a wonky slab or a door opening that's ten mil out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With both of you in construction, does that change your plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means we shouldn't both jump at the same time. One of us keeps the steady thing going while the other learns something new. Probably me jumping first, because Tom's work is more spread out.

S1.say: It will change how people work, so they'd better keep up; it's neither good nor bad. Firms should help people train and government should help those caught out.
S1.think: She's already seen a video of a machine that hangs plasterboard alone, and boarding is half her day. She won't panic but won't pretend it won't touch her.
S1.do: Waits to see the machine on a real site, then asks to be the person working alongside it and asks her employer to pay for training. Encourages her partner to learn building controls work.
S1.feel: Uneasy, like a draught under the door that will need fixing eventually.
S1.quote: Then on site you find out it can't handle a wonky slab or a door opening that's ten mil out.
S1.fieldNote: She thinks about change as a household, planning so the two of them don't jump at once. She wants proof on a real site before acting, then moves deliberately. Her politics are balanced: firms and government both have a part.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say nobody's ready for this and we need sensible help quickly, from employers and government both. Not a free-for-all, but not people losing their homes overnight either. I'd say that to anyone, but calmly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be frightened because it hits both of us at once. If robots can do fit-out and wiring in two years, our house is gone, simple as that. There's no 'one of us keeps the steady thing going' in this picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That first week I'd sit down with Tom and the bank app and cut everything we can, the gym, the streaming, Riya's extra tutoring maybe. I'd ring the mortgage lender early to ask what they'd do if we fell behind. I'd look for any job that still needs a person on the ground, even if it's site security or inspection, and I'd take the first one that's steady.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like being in a lift when the cable snaps. Not panic exactly, but my stomach would drop and stay dropped.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've got two years before it fully arrives. Would you use that time differently?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try to get a site inspector or clerk of works qualification, someone who checks the work's been done right. Robots or not, somebody's going to need to sign it off, at least for a while. But two years is tight with a full-time job and two kids.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned cutting Riya's tutoring. How would that conversation go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Badly. She's fifteen and wants to be a vet, and the tutoring's for her maths. I'd probably cut something of mine first and keep hers going as long as I could.

S2.say: Nobody is ready, so employers and government both need to give sensible help quickly: not a free-for-all, but not people losing homes overnight. She'd say this calmly to anyone.
S2.think: She'd be frightened because it hits both her and Tom at once; if robots do fit-out and wiring in two years, their house is gone. Her usual 'one of us stays steady' plan wouldn't work.
S2.do: Cuts the gym, streaming and possibly her daughter's tutoring, and rings the mortgage lender early. Works towards a site inspector or clerk of works qualification and takes the first steady job that still needs a person on the ground.
S2.feel: Alarmed, with her stomach dropping and staying dropped, though not quite panic.
S2.quote: There's no 'one of us keeps the steady thing going' in this picture.
S2.fieldNote: The double exposure of two construction incomes is what turns her from uneasy to alarmed. Her plan is level-headed: early contact with the lender, a move toward inspection work. She would protect her daughter's tutoring before her own spending.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough time to plan if we start now. Employers should give notice of what they're automating, and colleges should offer evening courses that people like me can actually get to. And some money to tide people over while they switch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, five years makes it feel like a problem I could solve. One of us retrains, one keeps working, we save what we can, and we're ready when it lands. It's not easy, but it's a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd sign up for the inspector course at the college, two evenings a week, and Tom would keep the electrical work going. We'd put whatever we can aside, even fifty a month, and stop the extras. By year three I'd want to be doing inspection work part-time, so I'm not starting from zero when it arrives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but steady. It's a lot of work, but I can see the steps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What changes for you between two years and five?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years we both drop at once. With five, we can take turns, which is the only way a family like ours gets through anything. That's the whole difference.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Darren, who's in his fifties and only knows boarding. He's a good lad, but he's never done a course in his life and he's got a sick wife. Five years won't be enough for him unless someone holds his hand.

S3.say: Five years is enough to plan if planning starts now: employers should give notice of what they're automating, colleges should offer accessible evening courses, and there should be money to tide people over.
S3.think: Five years makes it feel like a problem she could solve: one partner retrains, one keeps working, they save, and they're ready on arrival.
S3.do: Signs up for a college inspector course two evenings a week while Tom keeps the electrical work going. Saves what they can, stops extras, and aims to be doing part-time inspection work by year three.
S3.feel: Anxious but steady, able to see the steps.
S3.quote: With five, we can take turns, which is the only way a family like ours gets through anything.
S3.fieldNote: 'Taking turns' is the heart of Vera's approach, and the five-year timeline makes it possible again. Her plan is staged and realistic. She notices colleagues who'd struggle, like Darren, without making it political.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time, so let's do it sensibly. Businesses should plan, people should retrain, and the government should keep a safety net for anyone left behind. No need for drama.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years feels manageable. Riya and Kai would be grown or nearly, the mortgage would be smaller, and I'd have time to move into inspection or something like it without a rush. It's the version where we don't have to gamble.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait a couple of years to see which new jobs are actually being created, then pick a course. Meanwhile I'd keep working, build up savings a little, and get Tom to look at the building controls side. I'd also talk to Riya and Kai about choosing subjects with a bit of an eye on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly fine. It feels like something we can handle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With ten years, would you still wait before acting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, yes. With that long, the first courses that come out will probably be rubbish. I'd rather watch for two years and pick the one that's working for people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Riya about becoming a vet, if machines can do almost any work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her to go for it, because animals and their owners are going to want a person. But I'd also say, keep your eyes open and learn to use the machines, because the vets who do that will do better. And I'd tell her I'm proud of her either way.

S4.say: Ten years is plenty of time to do it sensibly: businesses plan, people retrain and the government keeps a safety net for anyone left behind, with no need for drama.
S4.think: Ten years feels manageable: children grown or nearly, a smaller mortgage and time to move into inspection work without a rush. It's the version where they don't have to gamble.
S4.do: Waits a couple of years to see which new jobs actually appear, then picks a course. Keeps working, builds savings, nudges Tom toward building controls and talks with the children about subject choices.
S4.feel: Uneasy but mostly fine, as if it's something they can handle.
S4.quote: It's the version where we don't have to gamble.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade, she slows down deliberately, expecting the first courses to be poor and preferring to pick a proven one. Family planning is central again, especially her daughter's ambition to be a vet. Her tone stays balanced and practical throughout.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because it would take both of our incomes at once and there'd be no one to keep things steady. What would help is a bridge: a year of income support tied to retraining, and lenders being made to give families like ours some breathing room instead of repossessing straight away.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You could ask about couples where both people are in the same trade. There's loads of us in construction, we meet on site. Nobody plans for the fact that when building stops, two pay packets stop at once.

headlineQuote: Nobody plans for the fact that when building stops, two pay packets stop at once.
portrait: Vera Gupta is a 43-year-old fit-out carpenter putting up partitions and ceilings in a school extension, married to a self-employed electrician, with two children and less than a month saved. She uses AI now and then and wants to see new kit work on a real site before trusting it. She's calm in AI Plateau and uneasy in Steady Disruption, planning to work alongside the boarding machines. AGI by 2028 alarms her because it would hit both incomes at once, while five or ten years let the couple 'take turns' as she moves into inspection work. Her views are pragmatic: employers, colleges and government all have a part to play.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because it would take both household incomes at once with no one to keep things steady.
whatWouldHelp: A year of income support tied to retraining, and lenders being required to give families breathing room rather than repossessing straight away.
